S053-01.notes: Contrast with 'lucid' plus 'folding clause into clause until readers must go back' = convoluted. A laconic (terse) is the opposite of long, nested sentences. B colloquial concerns informal register, not complexity. C effusive means gushing in emotion, not structurally tangled.

S053-02.notes: The same thinning at a village without the wheel undercuts the wheel as the sole cause, so another factor may have contributed. A contradicts 'never adopted the wheel.' C contradicts the same thinning at the second village. D contradicts the observed thinning and greater uniformity.

S053-03.notes: Text 2 proposes a different function (signaling defenses to insects), so the ecologists would offer an alternative function. B is too strong; Text 2 never denies sunscreen protection. C misattributes the regional pattern, which Text 2 explains with insects. D: yellow-leaf nutrient recovery is never discussed.

S053-04.notes: 62->74->79->81 gives gains of 12, 5 and 2, which supports both parts of the claim (higher scores and shrinking gains). A gives only the top group. B supports only the 'more study, higher score' part. D gives a total and says nothing about diminishing gains.

S053-05.notes: The text introduces pointed eggs, raises a problem for the cliff-ledge explanation (ground nesters), then reports the flight-ability study. A is backwards; the text rejects the traditional explanation. B: there is no detailed comparison of nesting habits. C: the measurement methods are not explained.

S053-06.notes: A colon after an independent clause introduces the noun phrase that names the cause. A: a semicolon needs an independent clause after it, but 'a fungus that had been carried...' is only a noun phrase. C makes a comma splice: '...decline, it was a fungus...'. D gives 'decline, which a fungus that had been carried...', where the relative clause has no verb and so is ungrammatical.

S053-07.notes: Inverted sentence whose subject is 'several species of willow' (plural), so the verb is 'grow.' A, B and D are all singular verb forms; the nearby singular nouns 'riverbank' and 'spring' are the intended trap. The tense of D is not the problem; its number is.

S053-08.notes: The second sentence restates and defines 'sunny-day flooding,' so 'In other words' fits. B Nevertheless signals a contrast that isn't there. C Similarly would require a separate, parallel phenomenon. D As a result wrongly treats the streets filling as a consequence of the flooding, when it is the flooding itself.
